summary: RFC 6282 defines header compression for 6LoWPAN packets. This document adds a simple way to compress generic headers and header-like payloads, without a new compression scheme for each new one.

plainLanguage.summary: Small wireless devices that carry Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) traffic spend much of every packet on headers. This RFC gives those networks one compression scheme that can shrink any header, not only the ones thought of in advance. The sender replaces repeated parts of a header with short instructions that point back at bytes it has already sent.

questions: how does generic header compression work in 6lowpan
subtitle: One compression scheme for any 6LoWPAN header, so a new header no longer needs a new specification.

tldr.problem: Header compression schemes normally need a separate specification for every kind of header they compress. The 6LoWPAN scheme in RFC 6282 had no way to be extended, so each candidate header reopened and reexamined that document.
tldr.mechanism: Generic Header Compression defines a small bytecode of five instructions: copy literal bytes, copy a run of zero bytes, stop, set up a backreference, and perform the backreference. It plugs into the Next Header Compression framework of RFC 6282 as a format for UDP payloads, ICMPv6 payloads and extension headers.
tldr.outcome: One scheme now covers headers of any kind and header-like payloads such as routing messages, so adding a header type no longer means writing a new specification. The RFC also adds a neighbour discovery option that tells a node whether its neighbour can decode the compressed form.

facts.label: Dictionary size
facts.value: 48 bytes: the 32 bytes of the two IPv6 addresses plus a 16-byte static dictionary

today: RFC 7400 is a Proposed Standard from November 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it stands as the definition of generic header compression for 6LoWPAN. It builds on the compression scheme in RFC 6282 and is meant to work alongside the neighbour discovery rules in RFC 6775.

sections.title: One Scheme Per Header Does Not Scale
sections.content:
Header compression schemes normally need a new specification for every kind of header they compress. RFC 6282, which defines 6LoWPAN Header Compression (6LoWPAN-HC), also defines no extensibility mechanism of the kind the Robust Header Compression (ROHC) profiles have. The result was that 6LoWPAN-HC was reopened and reexamined every time a new header was considered, or an old one was changed. Publishing RFC 6282 did not remove the underlying problem.

This document adds Generic Header Compression (GHC) to RFC 6282 without changing RFC 6282, using its Next Header Compression (NHC) concept. GHC is deliberately a little less efficient than a scheme built for one header, but it is far more general: it applies to headers of any kind, and to header-like payloads such as those carried by routing protocols and DHCP. The stated goal is a specification that fits on one page and can be implemented in a small number of lines of code, rather than a general data compression scheme such as DEFLATE.
sections.plainLanguage: Compressing packet headers normally means writing a separate specification for each header type, and RFC 6282 had no way to add one later. This document adds one general scheme instead, so a new header type no longer needs a new document.

sections.title: The Compression Approach
sections.content:
The compression function of GHC is a bytecode: a series of simple instructions that tell a decompressor how to rebuild the original payload. The instructions append bytes given literally in the compressed data, append a given number of zero bytes, and append bytes by copying a contiguous sequence from the payload being rebuilt, which is called backreferencing. A fourth instruction sets up parameters for the backreference in variables called the decompression variables. A stop code ends the compressed data.

The buffer that the decompressor fills is prefixed with a predefined dictionary that backreferences can use as if it were a prefix of the payload. The dictionary is built from the IPv6 source and destination addresses of the packet being rebuilt, followed by a static component, the static dictionary. The specification defines the decompressor in detail and leaves the compressor open to implementations: it can be a classical LZ77 compressor, or a simple protocol encoder that uses known compression opportunities.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme works like this. The sender sends a list of short instructions instead of the header itself. One instruction copies bytes, one adds a run of zero bytes, and one points back at bytes already written earlier. The receiver follows the instructions and rebuilds the original header exactly.

sections.title: The Five GHC Instructions
sections.content:
A compressed header is a sequence of pieces. Each piece starts with a code byte and may be followed by zero or more bytes of argument. Some code bytes lay bytes out in the destination buffer; others only change the decompression variables.

At the start of decompressing a header or payload within a layer 2 packet, the decompression variables sa and na are set to zero. The code byte templates are as follows. 0kkkkkkk appends k bytes of data given in the bytecode argument, where k is less than 96. 1000nnnn appends 0b0000nnnn plus two zero bytes. 10010000 is the stop code. 101nssss sets up extended arguments for a backreference by adding to sa and na. 11nnnkkk is the backreference itself: it copies n bytes from bytes already output, starting s bytes to the left of the current output position, and then resets sa and na to zero.

For backreferences, the expansion buffer starts with the predefined dictionary: the source and destination IPv6 addresses of the packet, followed by a 16-byte static dictionary. Those 48 dictionary bytes can be referenced but are not copied into the final payload. The bit patterns 011xxxxx, and 1001nnnn where 0b0000nnnn is greater than zero, are reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: Each compressed header is a run of instructions, one byte each, sometimes followed by data bytes. There are five kinds: copy literal bytes, copy zeros, stop, prepare a backreference, and perform the backreference. The decoder starts each header with two counters set to zero.

sections.title: Fitting GHC into 6LoWPAN Header Compression
sections.content:
GHC plugs in as an NHC format for 6LoWPAN-HC. Because GHC is generic, a single NHC value suffices to define an NHC format for ICMPv6 based on GHC, and many of the examples in the appendix are for ICMPv6 packets. An NHC format for UDP is also useful, because header-like payloads such as DHCPv6 and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) are carried in UDP. RFC 6282 already defines an NHC format for UDP, 11110CPP. GHC uses the analogous NHC byte 11010CPP. The difference is that for 11010CPP NHC bytes the UDP payload is not supplied literally but compressed by 6LoWPAN-GHC. To stay in the same numbering space, 11011111 is used for ICMPv6 GHC.

Extension headers are handled in a similar way, with the NHC byte 10110EEN. There is no easy way to extract the Length field from a GHC-encoded header before decoding it, so the Length field is elided entirely, in the same way NHC already elides the Next Header field in certain cases, and is reconstructed only on decompression. The bytecode 0b10010000 serves as the terminator for the extension header. The stop code is only needed for extension headers, because decompression of a final payload stops automatically at the end of the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: GHC attaches to the existing 6LoWPAN compression rules through what the RFC calls Next Header Compression. UDP payloads, ICMPv6 payloads and extension headers each get their own one-byte marker telling the receiver that what follows is compressed.

sections.title: Telling a Neighbour That GHC Is Available
sections.content:
Before a node can send GHC-compressed packets to a neighbour, it needs to know that the neighbour implements GHC. The 6LoWPAN baseline includes only RFC 4944, RFC 6282 and RFC 6775, and this document does not want to disturb RFC 6775, so it defines a Neighbor Discovery (ND) option: the 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option (6CIO). Its G bit indicates whether the node sending the option is GHC capable.

A node can also learn the capability implicitly, by receiving a packet from the neighbour that contains GHC. Something has to bootstrap that, since nobody would send a GHC packet first. Once a node has received either an explicit or an implicit indication of GHC capability, it may send GHC-compressed packets to that node. Where the capability has not been recently confirmed, a node SHOULD make use of Neighbor Unreachability Detection failures to switch back to basic 6LoWPAN header compression.

The 6CIO will typically only be sent in 6LoWPAN-ND Router Solicitation packets, which cannot themselves be GHC compressed unless the host limits itself to talking to GHC-capable routers. The resulting Router Advertisement can then make use of GHC, which indicates the capability implicitly, and that in turn allows both nodes to use GHC in the Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement exchange. Bits that IANA has not assigned MUST be sent as zero and MUST be ignored on reception. Length values larger than 1 MUST be accepted so that the option can be extended, with the extra bits treated as unassigned. Flag numbers 0 to 7 are reserved for experimental use and MUST NOT be used for actual deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: A node may only send compressed packets to a neighbour once it knows the neighbour can decode them. The RFC adds a small option to the neighbour discovery messages that carries one bit saying that the sender understands GHC, and a node can also learn this just by seeing a GHC packet arrive.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4944 and RFC 6282 apply. As in any protocol that parses and builds packets, implementations must avoid buffer overflows and, in particular for backreferencing, out-of-area references during decompression.

An attacker may send a forged packet that makes one node believe a third node is GHC capable when it is not. That can prevent packets sent by the second node from reaching the third node, at least until the robustness features of Section 3.3 take effect. No mitigation is proposed for this attack, and a victim node that does implement GHC is not vulnerable to it. With secured ND the 6CIO is secured too, so nodes relying on secured ND should use the 6CIO bidirectionally and limit the implicit capability detection to secured ND packets carrying GHC.

As with any LZ77 scheme, decompression bombs, meaning compressed packets crafted to expand so much that the decompressor is overloaded, are a problem. The worst-case amplification of GHC is 17, so a full-size packet can be generated from a 6LoWPAN packet of 76 bytes. The 6LoWPAN network is still constrained, so the amplification at the edge router turns an entire 250 kbit/s 802.15.4 network, assuming a theoretical upper bound of 225 kbit/s throughput to a single-hop adjacent node, into a 3.8 Mbit/s attacker.

In a 6LoWPAN stack, sensitive information will normally be protected by transport-layer, application-layer or IP-layer security, all of which sit above the adaptation layer and so leave nothing sensitive to compress at the GHC level. A deployment that depends entirely on Media Access Control (MAC) layer security may be vulnerable to attacks that exploit redundancy disclosed by compression to recover information about secret values. The attacker would need to be in radio range and, since compression is stateless, would need to entice the sender of the secret value to also send a value the attacker controls in the same packet. All of these attacks are mitigated by some form of network access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression creates its own risks. A small packet can expand to a much larger one, so an attacker on the radio can make a node do far more work than the packet it received deserved. The RFC also notes that a forged packet can make one node believe another understands GHC, which silently stops traffic from reaching it.

sections.title: Worked Examples From Packet Captures
sections.content:
Appendix A of the RFC works through examples derived from actual packet captures taken at interoperability events. An RPL DODAG Information Solicitation payload of 8 bytes compresses to 6 bytes, a compression factor of 1.33. A longer RPL DODAG Information Object of 92 bytes compresses to 52 bytes, a factor of 1.77, and the RFC notes that the compressed output exposes an inefficiency in the simple-minded compressor used to generate it. A RPL Destination Advertisement Object of 50 bytes compresses to 27 bytes, a factor of 1.85.

Among the Neighbor Discovery messages, a Neighbor Solicitation of 48 bytes compresses to 26 bytes, a factor of 1.85, a Neighbor Advertisement of 48 bytes compresses to 27 bytes, a factor of 1.78, a Router Solicitation of 24 bytes compresses to 12 bytes, a factor of 2.00, and a Router Advertisement of 96 bytes compresses to 58 bytes, a factor of 1.66.

The DTLS examples show the effect of the static dictionary. A DTLS application data packet with 13 bytes of cleartext and 8 bytes of authenticator goes from 42 bytes to 27 bytes, a reduction of 15 bytes. A DTLS handshake packet carrying a client hello goes from 67 bytes to 53 bytes, because there is little to compress in the 32 bytes of randomness it holds.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC runs real captured packets through the scheme and reports the results. A neighbour discovery message of 48 bytes becomes 26 bytes. A routing message of 92 bytes becomes 52 bytes. The savings are smaller for messages that are mostly random data, because there is little repetition to point at.

items.label: Literal bytes
items.desc: Append k bytes of data given in the bytecode argument, where k is less than 96.

items.label: Stop code
items.desc: Ends the compressed data. Needed for extension headers.

items.label: Set up backreference
items.desc: Adds to sa and na, the two variables that extend the next backreference.

items.label: Backreference
items.desc: Copies n bytes from s bytes to the left of the current output position.

The UDP payload is compressed with GHC, not given literally

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the option. Values larger than 1 must be accepted.

fields.name: Unassigned flags
fields.desc: Flag numbers 0 to 14. Flag numbers 0 to 7 are reserved for experimental use.

fields.name: G bit
fields.desc: Flag number 15. Set when the sending node is GHC capable.

fields.name: Unassigned flags
fields.desc: Flag numbers 16 to 47. Unassigned bits must be sent as zero and ignored on reception.
